objective: Label every case in the lab with its validation-hierarchy tier so the trust a result may carry is bounded by its tier on the record
rationale: Oberkampf and Trucano organize validation as a building-block hierarchy: unit problems, benchmark cases, subsystem cases, complete system, with experimental information degrading radically up the tiers. The lab's portfolio maps cleanly: the laminar cylinder is a unit problem, the TMR flat plate and the motorcycle are benchmark cases, the valve screen is a subsystem case, the airliner is the complete-system posture where data are scarcest. Making the tier a named field beside the fidelity chip states why the airliner stops below VALIDATED no matter how tight its envelope, as a structural fact rather than a hedge. This is a content addition and may land directly on the certificate and wall surfaces.
citations: Verification And Validation In Computational Fluid Dynamics, Oberkampf And Trucano, Sandia Report SAND2002-0529
expected_knowledge_gain: A tier label per case that explains the ceiling on its fidelity chip and tells the owner exactly which tier new experimental data would unlock
outcome: All 24 cases the lab holds are placed in the building-block hierarchy: 8 unit problems, 11 benchmark cases, 2 subsystem cases and 3 complete-system cases, each carrying the basis for its placement, what data can exist at that tier, the ceiling that puts on its fidelity chip, and the single thing that would unlock the next tier. The field is named validation_tier and never tier, because tier already means the fidelity chip everywhere in this codebase, and the artifact deliberately carries no chip of its own: a second copy of a grade is a second thing to drift. Three of the 24, the CRM wing-body, the NASA hump and the ONERA M6, have no entry in the ratified display-name registry, and the record declares which three rather than inventing names beside them. A test regenerates the artifact and fails if it drifts from the module behind it.
